extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and business leaders
extracted.subtask_description: A roundup of high-profile public relations disasters from 2023 used to illustrate common failure modes and what to avoid; aimed at practitioners and leaders looking to learn from others' mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational safety and product/service competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the product or service is safe, technically competent, and does not endanger customers or users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: OceanGate 'sub had imploded before it even made it to the ocean floor' — a catastrophic operational failure that became a major PR disaster. The page highlights that credibility partnerships (NASA, University of Washington) can mask operational risks; operational safety lapses lead to rescue/recovery stories and public outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate professional advisors for public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose advisors whose skills match the forum — legal strategies that work in courtrooms may not work for public audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Former UPenn President Elizabeth Magill 'prepared for a congressional hearing ... with the help of $1,500 per hour attorneys instead of $500 per hour PR professionals' resulting in a 'debacle so bad that she was forced to resign.' Guidance: use communications counsel for public-facing events rather than relying solely on legal counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid offensive, discriminatory, or extremist public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures and brands must avoid statements that are racist, sexist, or otherwise offensive — such statements can destroy reputations and revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Scott Adams made racist comments that 'set the “Dilbert” industrial complex completely ablaze' and newspapers dropped his strip. Guidance: monitor and constrain individual/public-facing voices associated with your brand; treat inflammatory speech as a reputational threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate cultural and political backlash to marketing choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how marketing partners, influencers, or campaigns may provoke cultural or political reactions that can lead to boycotts and lost sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bud Light's inclusion of transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney triggered a successful boycott; sales dropped and company performance suffered. Guidance: run risk assessments for culturally sensitive campaigns and prepare mitigation plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic governance and long-term decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Make strategic choices that preserve an organization's long-term viability; avoid gambles that risk existential damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: PAC-12 'bet its existence on a game of chicken and lost' — poor strategic decisions and an ill-fated network contributed to its collapse. Guidance: align governance, revenue strategy, and contingency planning to avoid catastrophic organizational outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content moderation and advertiser safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms must manage extremism and hateful content to avoid advertiser flight and devaluation of the business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Elon Musk/X 'embrace of antisemites...caused most mainstream advertisers...to finally walk away' and devalued the company. Guidance: maintain robust moderation policies and protect brand-safety to retain advertising partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability of user engagement beyond launch
rubrics_metrics.description: New products and platforms must translate initial growth into sustained usage; ephemeral launch spikes are not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Threads was 'the fastest-growing app' but 'usage dropped by nearly 80%.' Guidance: plan for retention, product-market fit, and long-term engagement strategies, not only launch publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder and political reputational management
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures and board members must monitor and manage local political support and public perception, and act on poor polling or support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Auon’tai Anderson had just 9% support and quickly chose not to run for re-election. Guidance: read political winds, address constituent concerns early, and avoid actions that magnify low public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership accountability for personal misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must promptly and transparently address leaders' misconduct; failure to do so intensifies public backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Spain’s soccer federation president forcibly kissed a player and was widely condemned; under pressure he 'resigned.' Guidance: swift accountability, credible investigatory process, and clear sanctioning reduce prolonged reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial integrity and ethical use of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations must maintain fact-checking, attribution, and transparency when using AI; fabrications or undisclosed AI content harm credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sports Illustrated was 'accused of publishing AI-generated stories' and subsequently fired executives. Guidance: implement editorial safeguards, audit AI outputs, and disclose use of AI to avoid fraud-like accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and financial risk communication during disasters
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing large-scale liabilities, companies must proactively communicate legal exposure and remediation plans to stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hawaiian Electric expected 'as many as 1,000 lawsuits' after Maui wildfires and saw severe stock declines. Guidance: coordinate legal, financial, and communications teams to present transparent, compassionate, and factual responses to mitigate investor and public fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic financial communications and investment narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: New investments and renovations should be accompanied by realistic public financial expectations to avoid public skepticism about returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Casa Bonita owners 'spent $40 million renovating' and the post frames revenue targets to recoup investment. Guidance: avoid overpromising, be transparent about business plans, and contextualize large expenditures for stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between stated values and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should align their public moral/ethical positions with actual behaviors and partnerships; hypocrisy erodes trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: PGA Tour spent years making moral arguments against LIV Golf only to merge with it, 'blindsiding its own golfers' and causing feelings of betrayal. Guidance: be consistent in values-based communications and inform internal stakeholders before public announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely, direct communication with affected stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications about major changes should be delivered promptly and directly to those most affected rather than revealed indirectly via media or social channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: PGA Tour golfers 'learn[ing] about the merger on social media' exacerbated feelings of betrayal. Guidance: prioritize direct briefings for internal stakeholders and key partners prior to public disclosure.
